question.prompt: For all integers \(n\) greater than \(1,\) define \[a_n=\dfrac{1}{\log_n 2002}.\] Let \(b=a_2+a_3+a_4+a_5\) and \(c=a_{10}+a_{11}+a_{12}+a_{13}+a_{14}.\) Then \(b-c\) equals

solutions.explanation:
The varying logarithm bases make the sums awkward. Change every term to the same base so that logarithm rules can combine them.

For \(n>1\), both logarithms are defined and \(\log_n2002>0\), so its reciprocal is valid. Using \(\log\) for the base-ten logarithm, change of base gives
\[
a_n=\frac{\log n}{\log2002}=\log_{2002}n.
\]
The sum and difference rules for logarithms now give
\[
b-c=\log_{2002}\left(
\frac{2\cdot3\cdot4\cdot5}
{10\cdot11\cdot12\cdot13\cdot14}
\right).
\]
Since \(2\cdot3\cdot4\cdot5=10\cdot12\), these factors cancel, leaving
\[
b-c=\log_{2002}\left(\frac1{11\cdot13\cdot14}\right)
=\log_{2002}(2002^{-1})
=\boxed{-1}.
\]
The answer is choice \(\boxed{\text{B}}\).
solutions.title: Rewrite every term with one base
